title: HLA and the Transplant Crossmatch: DSA, PRA and False Positives
summary: Place HLA class I and II on the immune map, see how patients become sensitized, read CDC and flow crossmatches, and use PRA, single-antigen beads and DTT to separate dangerous donor-specific antibody from false positives.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 50 Hits 2, 4, 5 and 6 and Trap 2 (first lesson for Ch. 50). Checked against Zarei 2026 and Althaf 2017. Nuance: the reviewer calls a positive current-serum CDC crossmatch an “absolute contraindication”; Althaf’s risk table grades DTT-negative IgM/autoreactive positives as standard risk and describes lupus false positives (register rv-cdc-absolute). Not taught as fact: peptide lengths, β2-microglobulin chromosome, sibling 1-in-4 inheritance, allele counts, graft survival figures, 10/10 HCT matching, typing-method order, Bw4/Bw6 and CREG figures, current vs historic serum (Hits 1, 3, 7–14; Traps 1, 3–6).

objectives: Contrast HLA class I and class II by loci and the T cells they engage, and name the routes of sensitization.
Interpret CDC and flow crossmatch patterns, including T + B versus B-only reactivity.
Explain PRA, cPRA, virtual crossmatch, and how DTT and beads resolve false positives.

scenes.title: A positive crossmatch
scenes.altText: Case adapted from a published worked example (Althaf 2017): a young man with end-stage kidney disease from lupus nephritis is offered a deceased-donor kidney. The complement-dependent cytotoxicity (CDC) crossmatch is POSITIVE with B lymphocytes. Question token: “Is the transplant off?”

cues.text: A young man with kidney failure from lupus is offered a deceased-donor kidney.
The crossmatch, which tests his serum against the donor’s lymphocytes, comes back positive with B cells.
Is the transplant off? What else does the laboratory need to know?

scenes.title: HLA classes and how patients become sensitized
scenes.altText: Map card (Zarei 2026): HLA genes lie on the short arm of chromosome 6 (6p21). Class I (HLA-A, -B, -C) present peptides from INSIDE the cell to cytotoxic CD8⁺ T cells; class II (HLA-DP, -DQ, -DR) present antigens from OUTSIDE the cell to CD4⁺ helper T cells, which help antibody-producing B cells; the class III region includes complement C2 and C4. Sensitization card (Althaf 2017): anti-HLA antibodies usually arise after pregnancy, blood transfusion or a previous transplant; almost a third of wait-listed patients have some anti-HLA antibody.

cues.text: HLA genes sit on the short arm of chromosome 6. Class I molecules, HLA-A, B and C, show peptides from inside the cell to CD8 cytotoxic T cells.
Class II molecules, HLA-DP, DQ and DR, show antigens taken up from outside to CD4 helper T cells, which in turn help B cells make antibody.
A patient can make antibodies against another person’s HLA. The usual routes are pregnancy, blood transfusion and a previous transplant.
Almost a third of patients on a transplant waiting list have some anti-HLA antibody.

scenes.title: Donor-specific antibody and the crossmatch
scenes.altText: Risk card (Althaf 2017): high titres of donor-specific HLA antibody (DSA) at transplant can cause hyperacute rejection; donor-specific cytotoxic antibody (positive crossmatch) was historically a contraindication. Even low-titre DSA can cause early or late antibody-mediated rejection. Assay card: CDC crossmatch — recipient serum + donor lymphocytes + complement; antibody bound at adequate density activates complement, cells die and take up dye. Flow cytometry crossmatch (FCXM) detects bound antibody without needing cell death. Pattern (Althaf 2017 risk table): T- AND B-cell positive with IgG → class I DSA; B-cell-only positive with IgG → class II DSA.

cues.text: The danger is antibody against the donor’s own HLA, called donor-specific antibody. At high titre it can destroy a transplanted kidney almost immediately: hyperacute rejection.
The classic test is the CDC crossmatch: recipient serum, donor lymphocytes and complement. If enough antibody binds, complement kills the cells and they take up dye.
A flow cytometry crossmatch detects bound antibody directly, without needing the cells to die, so it picks up weaker antibody.
Which cells react matters. Killing of both T and B cells by IgG points to a class I antibody; B cells alone point to class II.

props.label: FCXM: detects binding, no killing needed

props.title: Which cells react (IgG)
lines: T + B positive → class I DSA

scenes.title: Screening, virtual crossmatch, and false positives
scenes.altText: Screen card (Althaf 2017): PRA (panel-reactive antibody) — percentage of a cell panel killed — approximates a recipient’s risk of a positive crossmatch with a donor from a similar population; it depends on the panel used. Single-antigen beads (SAB, Luminex) list distinct antibody specificities; comparing them with HLA frequencies in the donor population gives the calculated PRA (cPRA); SAB results enable a virtual crossmatch. Microbead assays are about 10% more sensitive than ELISA, which is about 10% more sensitive than AHG-enhanced CDC. Interference card: IgM or other serum factors (and IVIG) can interfere; dithiothreitol (DTT) and dilution help. Althaf risk table: a CDC positive that disappears with DTT reflects IgM, often autoreactive non-HLA, = standard risk. Worked case (Althaf 2017): B-cell CDC positive, FCXM negative for T and B cells, SAB no DSA → false positive from lupus immune complexes binding Fc receptors → standard immunological risk.

cues.text: Before any donor appears, patients are screened. The panel-reactive antibody estimates how likely a crossmatch is to be positive with donors from a similar population.
Single-antigen beads name each antibody. Comparing those with donor-population HLA frequencies gives the calculated PRA, and lets the lab run a virtual crossmatch against a donor’s typing.
Not every positive crossmatch is dangerous. IgM or other serum factors can cause positives; treating serum with DTT removes IgM. A positive that vanishes with DTT is standard risk.

In our lupus patient the flow crossmatch was negative and the beads found no donor-specific antibody: immune complexes had given a false-positive B-cell result. The transplant can proceed at standard risk.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “PRA 60% means a 60% chance of finding a donor” (✓ PRA approximates the chance of a POSITIVE crossmatch — high PRA = harder to find a compatible donor); “Every positive CDC crossmatch rules out transplant” (✓ check antibody class and specificity: DTT-negative IgM/autoreactive positives and lupus false positives are standard risk; IgG DSA at high titre is the veto); “A B-cell-only positive crossmatch means a class I antibody” (✓ B-only with IgG points to class II DSA; T + B points to class I).

cues.text: Trap one: a PRA of 60 percent means a 60 percent chance of finding a donor. No: it approximates the chance of a positive crossmatch. Higher PRA, harder to find a compatible donor.

Trap two: every positive CDC crossmatch rules out transplant. No: check the antibody. IgM that disappears with DTT, or a lupus false positive, is standard risk. High-titre IgG donor-specific antibody is the veto.
Trap three: a B-cell-only positive crossmatch means a class I antibody. No: B cells alone point to class II; T and B together point to class I.

props.title: ✗ “B-only positive = class I.”
lines: ✓ B only → class II · T + B → class I

scenes.title: Who bites, and does DTT stop it?
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Both T and B bitten → class I; only B bitten → class II. If DTT stops the bite, it was IgM — usually harmless. If beads name a donor antigen, it is real.” Tokens: T + B = I · B = II · DTT-neg = IgM · beads name DSA. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: both T and B cells bitten means class I; only B cells bitten means class II. If DTT stops the bite, it was IgM, usually harmless. If the beads name a donor antigen, the antibody is real.

Where it breaks: low-titre donor-specific IgG can still harm a graft later, even when the CDC is negative; risk categories differ between centres and depend on antibody history; and beads can show interference too, from IgM, other serum factors or IVIG.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Class I (A, B, C) → CD8 · class II (DP, DQ, DR) → CD4 · sensitized by pregnancy, transfusion, transplant”, “Crossmatch: T + B IgG = class I DSA, B only = class II · DTT-negative IgM or lupus false + = standard risk · PRA ≈ chance of positive crossmatch”.

cues.text: A crossmatch is dangerous when it reflects donor-specific IgG HLA antibody, so the laboratory separates true DSA from IgM, autoreactive or immune-complex false positives using DTT, flow cytometry and single-antigen beads.

props.label: Class I → CD8 · class II → CD4 · pregnancy, transfusion, transplant
T+B = class I · B = class II · DTT-neg IgM = standard risk

explanation.what: Plain language: a transplant can be destroyed by antibodies the recipient already has against the donor’s tissue type, so the laboratory looks for them before surgery — and must tell real danger from harmless look-alikes. Scientific terms: HLA class I/II, CD8/CD4, sensitization, donor-specific antibody (DSA), hyperacute rejection, antibody-mediated rejection, CDC crossmatch, flow cytometry crossmatch, PRA, cPRA, single-antigen beads, virtual crossmatch, dithiothreitol (DTT).
explanation.why: Pre-formed IgG against donor HLA binds the graft and can activate complement. In a crossmatch, the same antibody binds donor lymphocytes; IgM or immune complexes can mimic this without targeting donor HLA, so the antibody’s class and specificity decide the risk.
explanation.measure: CDC and FCXM crossmatches; T + B IgG positive → class I DSA, B-only → class II (Althaf 2017 table). PRA approximates positive-crossmatch risk; SAB specificities + donor HLA frequencies → cPRA; SAB enables virtual crossmatch. DTT removes IgM; DTT-negative positives are standard risk. Sensitivity: microbead > ELISA > AHG-CDC (~10% steps).
explanation.differs: True IgG DSA (high risk) vs DTT-sensitive IgM/autoreactive or immune-complex positives (standard risk); class I DSA (T + B) vs class II DSA (B only); PRA (cell panel) vs cPRA (bead specificities vs donor frequencies).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: interpret a high PRA, localize class I vs II from T/B crossmatch results, name sensitizing events, and recognize that DTT-negative or lupus-related positives are not true DSA.

questions.stem: A CDC crossmatch is positive with both T and B lymphocytes and remains positive after DTT treatment. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: IgG donor-specific antibody against HLA class I — high risk
options.rationale: Correct. T + B reactivity that persists after DTT fits IgG class I DSA (Althaf 2017 risk table).
Incorrect. IgM reactivity would disappear with DTT.
Incorrect. Class II DSA typically gives B-cell-only positivity.
Incorrect. Cell killing shows complement was active.

questions.stem: A wait-listed patient has a PRA of 85%. What does this mean?

options.text: A positive crossmatch is likely with most donors from a similar population, so finding a compatible donor is harder
options.rationale: Correct. PRA approximates the risk of a positive crossmatch.

options.text: There is an 85% chance of finding a compatible donor
options.rationale: Incorrect. This reverses the meaning of PRA.

options.text: The patient has 85% of normal antibody levels
options.rationale: Incorrect. PRA measures reactivity against a panel, not total antibody.

options.text: 85% of the patient’s HLA antigens are mismatched with the panel
options.rationale: Incorrect. PRA reflects antibody reactivity, not HLA typing mismatch.

questions.stem: Which event is a recognized route to HLA sensitization?

options.rationale: Correct. Pregnancy, blood transfusion and previous transplantation are the usual routes.
Incorrect. This does not expose the patient to foreign HLA.

options.text: Receiving an autologous stem-cell transplant only
options.rationale: Incorrect. Autologous cells carry the patient’s own HLA.
Incorrect. Not a usual route of anti-HLA alloimmunization.
